prompt: Write an essay explaining how public-key cryptography works. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
Public-key cryptography, also called asymmetric cryptography, is a method of securing information in which each participant holds a pair of related keys rather than a single shared secret. One key, the public key, may be distributed freely. The other, the private key, must remain known only to its owner. Operations performed with one key can be undone only with the other. That asymmetry is what lets strangers communicate securely over an open network, and what lets a recipient verify that a message really came from a claimed sender.

The problem it solves is older than computers. With traditional symmetric cryptography, the same key encrypts and decrypts. If Alice and Bob have never met, they cannot safely agree on that key by shouting it across a channel an eavesdropper can hear. In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman described how two parties could establish a shared secret by exchanging information that, by itself, does not reveal the secret. Soon afterward, Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir, and Leonard Adleman published the RSA system, which made encryption and digital signatures practical with a public and private key. Later systems based on elliptic curves achieved similar security with shorter keys. The details differ, but the architecture is the same.

The mathematical foundation is a one-way function with a trapdoor. A one-way function is easy to compute in one direction and believed to be infeasible to reverse with ordinary resources. The trapdoor is secret information that makes reversal easy for the key holder. In RSA, the public key includes a large number that is the product of two secret primes, together with an encryption exponent. Multiplying those primes is trivial; factoring their product, when they are hundreds or thousands of bits long, is not, with known classical algorithms and present computers. The private key encodes the relationship that lets its owner invert the encryption. Elliptic-curve systems rely on a different hard problem, the difficulty of recovering a secret multiplier from a point obtained by repeated addition on a curve, but they serve the same roles.

Key generation begins with random choices large enough to resist search. From those choices the algorithm derives the public and private keys so that they correspond. The public key can be posted on a website, printed on a business card, or stored in a directory. Anyone may use it. Confidentiality works as follows. Suppose Bob wants to send Alice a message that only she can read. He obtains Alice’s public key and transforms the message with it. The result, the ciphertext, can travel through untrusted networks. Eve, who sees the ciphertext and even Alice’s public key, cannot recover the plaintext without the private key, assuming the scheme is sound and the keys are long enough. Alice applies her private key and obtains the original message. If she loses that key, she cannot read messages encrypted to her; if someone else obtains it, they can.

The same pair supports authentication through digital signatures, with the roles reversed. Alice hashes her message, producing a short fingerprint, and transforms that fingerprint with her private key. The result is a signature. Anyone with her public key can check that the signature matches the message and could have been produced only by someone who holds the corresponding private key. If a single bit of the message changes, verification fails. Signatures therefore provide integrity as well as origin: the recipient learns both who apparently signed and that the content was not altered afterward. They do not, by themselves, prove that the public key belongs to the person named Alice. That binding is the job of certificates and trust.

A public-key certificate is a signed statement, usually from a certificate authority or from a peer in a web of trust, that a particular public key belongs to a particular identity. Browsers and operating systems ship with a set of trusted authority keys. When a website presents a certificate, the client checks the signature chain back to one of those anchors, and checks that the name in the certificate matches the site it intended to reach. If an attacker substitutes a different public key, the certificate check fails unless the attacker has also compromised an authority or tricked the user into trusting a forged key. This is why simply “using encryption” is not enough. Encryption to the wrong party is secure against outsiders and useless against the party who holds the matching private key.

In practice, public-key operations are slower and more cumbersome for bulk data than symmetric ciphers such as AES. Real systems are hybrid. A protocol such as the handshake in Transport Layer Security uses public-key methods, or a related key-agreement method, to authenticate the server and to establish a fresh symmetric session key. The actual web pages, email bodies, or file contents are then encrypted with that session key. Forward secrecy, common in modern handshakes, derives the session key in such a way that later compromise of a long-term private key does not reveal past sessions. Public-key cryptography also underpins software updates, secure email, cryptocurrencies, and code signing: wherever a system must check authenticity without a pre-shared secret.

The guarantees are conditional. They depend on the hardness of the underlying problem, on correct implementation, on good random numbers, and on private keys staying private. Side channels, flawed padding, weak parameters, and stolen keys have broken deployments even when the mathematics was sound. Quantum computers, if built at sufficient scale, would undermine RSA and current elliptic-curve schemes by solving their hard problems efficiently; researchers are therefore standardizing post-quantum algorithms based on other assumptions. None of that changes the idea that made the field possible. By separating a key that may be published from a key that must be hidden, and by tying them through a function that is easy one way and hard the other, public-key cryptography lets people who have never shared a secret still encrypt, sign, and agree on keys in public.
